title: THE BEDROOM WARNING MOST CHRISTIAN COUPLES NEVER HEAR: WHY DID PAUL SAY, “DO NOT DEPRIVE ONE ANOTHER”?
paragraphs: THE BEDROOM WARNING MOST CHRISTIAN COUPLES NEVER HEAR: WHY DID PAUL SAY, “DO NOT DEPRIVE ONE ANOTHER”?

What if one of the most misunderstood verses about marriage was never meant to give a spouse power over another—but to protect two hearts from the silent distance that can destroy a marriage? The original Greek reveals something every husband and wife needs to understand before love turns into resentment, intimacy becomes an obligation, and the enemy finds room in what God intended to be sacred.
There is a kind of loneliness that only married people understand.
It is lying beside someone you once could not wait to hold, yet feeling as though an ocean has formed between your bodies.
It is hearing, “Good night,” when what your heart desperately wants to ask is, “Are we still okay?”

It is being married on paper but emotionally separated by years of unresolved arguments, unspoken disappointments, physical exhaustion, rejection, shame, and wounds neither person knows how to explain.
Sometimes the distance begins with an argument.
Sometimes with a baby who never sleeps.
Sometimes with financial pressure, depression, illness, betrayal, or years of feeling unseen.
And sometimes it begins so quietly that neither husband nor wife remembers when affection stopped feeling natural.
Then one Sunday, someone opens a Bible and reads a verse that seems to settle everything.
“Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.”
—1 Corinthians 7:5, King James Version
And suddenly, a Scripture meant to guide married believers becomes a weapon in an already wounded home.
One spouse says, “See? The Bible says you cannot refuse me.”
The other thinks, “Does God even care about what I am going through?”
And somewhere between those two hearts, the actual meaning of Paul's words gets buried.
But here is what should stop every Christian husband and wife in their tracks.

Paul was not writing a permission slip for sexual entitlement. He was addressing a marriage relationship in which neither spouse was supposed to treat the other's needs, dignity, or spiritual well-being as insignificant.
And when we examine what Paul actually wrote in Greek, the passage becomes even more challenging.
Because it does not merely confront the spouse who withdraws.
It also confronts the spouse who demands.
To understand why, we must return to Corinth.
Imagine a city filled with commerce, competing philosophies, pagan religious practices, and deeply conflicting attitudes toward the human body.
Some people treated sexual appetite as something to indulge.
Others regarded abstinence as a mark of spiritual superiority.
The Corinthian church was learning how to follow Jesus in the middle of these competing ideas.
And believers had questions.
Serious questions.
Questions about marriage, celibacy, sexual temptation, holiness, and whether abstaining from marital intimacy might make someone more spiritual.
Paul begins the chapter by responding to matters the Corinthians had written about.
He writes:
—1 Corinthians 7:1, KJV
The expression “not to touch a woman” is widely understood in this context as a reference to sexual relations, not a prohibition against ordinary physical contact.
Scholars differ over whether Paul is quoting a Corinthian slogan or expressing a qualified preference for celibacy.
But the direction of his answer becomes clear.
He does not declare marital intimacy dirty.
He does not teach that husbands and wives become holier by permanently withdrawing from each other.
Instead, he reminds married believers that their relationship involves mutual responsibilities.
And then he says something extraordinarily countercultural.
“The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
—1 Corinthians 7:4, KJV
Read the second half again.
“Likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
In a world where wives could easily be treated as subordinate possessions, Paul explicitly gives the wife a corresponding claim within the marriage.
Not just the husband.
The wife, too.
The Greek wording reinforces the reciprocity.
The verb translated “hath power” is ἐξουσιάζει (exousiazei), from a word associated with exercising authority.
Paul uses the same construction for both spouses.
That matters.
Because anyone who uses verse 4 to claim absolute sexual authority over a wife while ignoring the husband's corresponding responsibility has already distorted the passage.
And anyone who reads the verse as permission to disregard a spouse's suffering has failed to read it through the love commanded by Christ.
Marriage is not a battlefield where one person wins control of the other's body.
It is a covenant in which two people are called to honor one another before God.
Then comes verse 5.
The warning.
The instruction.
The sentence that has been quoted in bedrooms, marriage counseling sessions, church discussions, and painful arguments for generations.
In Greek, Paul begins:
μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους
Mē apostereite allēlous.
A close translation is:
“Do not deprive one another.”
The verb ἀποστερεῖτε (apostereite) comes from apostereō, meaning to deprive, defraud, or withhold something due.
And ἀλλήλους (allēlous) means “one another.”
Not merely “wives, do not deprive your husbands.”
Not merely “husbands, do not deprive your wives.”
One another.
Paul's warning runs in both directions.
And that small Greek expression destroys the idea that the passage establishes a one-sided privilege.
The apostle is confronting a pattern of unilateral withholding within marriage.
He is not telling one spouse to disregard the other's physical condition, emotional distress, or personal safety.
He is addressing married believers who might treat prolonged sexual abstinence as a unilateral decision, even when that decision affects their shared covenant.
But why would Paul care so deeply about this?
Because sexual intimacy within marriage is not presented in Scripture merely as a biological release.
It belongs to a larger biblical picture of covenant union.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
That phrase, “one flesh,” is profoundly important.
The Hebrew is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
Basar echad.
Literally, “one flesh.”
It describes the profound union of husband and wife, a union that includes bodily intimacy but cannot be reduced to it.
They are not simply two individuals sharing a house.
They are called into a covenantal life together.
Their joys affect each other.
Their wounds affect each other.
Their choices affect each other.
Their bodies are not unrelated to their shared life.
And their emotional and spiritual relationship cannot be treated as irrelevant to their physical relationship.
That is why a marriage can have a beautiful house, a stable income, respectable children, and smiling Sunday photographs while quietly suffering behind closed doors.
The world sees a family.
God sees the people inside it.
He sees the husband who feels unwanted.
He sees the wife who feels pressured.
He sees the exhaustion neither knows how to communicate.
He sees the resentment hidden beneath polite conversation.
He sees the couple who once prayed together but now barely speak.
And the Lord who created marriage does not call either spouse to pretend those wounds do not exist.
But there is another Greek phrase in verse 5 that many people overlook.
Paul writes:
ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρόν
Ek symphōnou pros kairon.
It means, in context, “by mutual agreement for a time.”
The word symphōnou comes from a word meaning agreement or harmony.
It is related to the Greek family of words from which English gets “symphony.”
The image of musical harmony can help us remember the idea, although Paul is speaking specifically about agreement rather than making a musical illustration.
Two people coming into agreement.
Two voices taking each other seriously.
Two lives making a shared decision.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say that one spouse should announce a season of abstinence and expect the other to silently accept it.
He does not say that spiritual devotion gives someone permission to dismiss a spouse's concerns.
He says there should be agreement.
And he connects this particular temporary abstinence with prayer.
Some later Greek manuscript traditions, reflected in the King James Version, include “fasting and prayer.” Many modern critical editions of the Greek New Testament read simply “prayer.”
The textual difference is worth acknowledging because accuracy matters when we claim to explain God's Word.
Paul's central point remains clear in either reading.
He is describing a mutually agreed period of abstinence for spiritual devotion, followed by the resumption of marital intimacy.
He is not issuing a universal rule that every couple must have sexual relations on a particular schedule.
Nor is he saying that illness, childbirth recovery, trauma, physical pain, emotional distress, or other serious circumstances must be ignored.
Those situations require compassion, patience, honest communication, and sometimes professional help.
Mutual agreement cannot be manufactured through fear, threats, guilt, or spiritual intimidation.
And marital commitment does not erase the need for consent.
That distinction is not a modern attempt to weaken Scripture.
It is necessary to avoid turning Paul's teaching about mutuality into an excuse for coercion.
Because the same Bible that records 1 Corinthians 7 also commands husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
—Ephesians 5:25, KJV
How did Christ love the church?
By giving Himself.
Not by exploiting vulnerability.
Not by demanding comfort while ignoring suffering.
Not by crushing the weak.
He loved sacrificially.
He served.
He laid down His life.
And if a husband wants to understand his biblical responsibility, he must look beyond what he believes his wife owes him and ask whether his own love resembles the self-giving love of Jesus.
Likewise, a wife is not called to use affection as a tool of punishment or control.
Both spouses are called to pursue faithfulness, honesty, tenderness, and peace.
This is where the passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because it exposes more than sexual neglect.
It exposes selfishness.
The husband who quotes 1 Corinthians 7:5 to demand intimacy while refusing to address his wife's pain must examine his heart.
The wife who deliberately uses physical affection to punish her husband instead of addressing the conflict must examine her heart.
The spouse who has stopped communicating.
The spouse who refuses accountability.
The spouse who treats intimacy as a transaction.
The spouse who hides behind religious language because admitting the truth would require humility.
And the spouse who has been suffering silently because nobody ever taught them that love should also be gentle.
All of them need something deeper than winning an argument about a Bible verse.
They need truth.
They need grace.
They need the transforming work of Jesus Christ.
But we must be careful here.
Not every season without sexual intimacy is an act of sinful deprivation.
A person recovering from surgery is not necessarily rejecting their spouse.
A mother healing after childbirth is not failing God because her body needs time.
A husband struggling with depression or a medical condition is not automatically guilty of withholding.
A survivor of sexual trauma may need safety, healing, and patient support before physical closeness feels possible.
And a spouse facing abuse should never be told that this passage requires submission to sexual coercion.
Paul's warning against deprivation must never become a weapon against someone who is vulnerable.
God's Word should be interpreted faithfully, not used to silence suffering.
And when there is abuse, the priority is safety, accountability, and appropriate support—not pressuring the harmed spouse to resume intimacy.
This brings us to the reason Paul gives for his warning.
He says that couples should come together again:
“that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.”
—1 Corinthians 7:5, KJV
The Greek phrase includes:
ἵνα μὴ πειράζῃ ὑμᾶς ὁ Σατανᾶς
Hina mē peirazē hymas ho Satanas.
“So that Satan may not tempt you.”
Paul is recognizing that prolonged abstinence can create a particular temptation for some married believers, especially when self-control is already a struggle.
The word translated “incontinency” in the KJV refers here to a lack of self-control.
But we must not twist that into something Paul never says.
He does not say that a spouse becomes responsible for the other's adultery.
He does not say that sexual frustration excuses pornography, betrayal, manipulation, or violence.
He does not say that temptation removes personal moral responsibility.
James 1:14 teaches that each person is tempted when drawn away by their own desire.
A spouse who commits adultery remains accountable for that choice.
A spouse who consumes pornography remains accountable for that choice.
A spouse who becomes abusive remains accountable for that choice.
No one gets to blame their sin on the person they promised to love.
Paul is urging believers to take temptation seriously and to care for their marriage rather than allowing avoidable division to grow.
And sometimes that care begins with a conversation neither spouse wants to have.
“Are you unhappy with me?”
“Have I hurt you?”
“Do you feel safe with me?”
“Have I made you feel like your needs do not matter?”
“Is there something happening in your body or heart that I have not understood?”
“Can we talk without blaming each other?”
Those questions may not sound dramatic.
But in a marriage where silence has lasted for months, they can feel terrifying.
Because real intimacy requires more than physical availability.
It requires the courage to be known.
And being known means risking honesty.
Maybe that is why some couples find it easier to argue about how often they should be intimate than to admit how deeply they have hurt each other.
A husband may say, “You never want me anymore,” when what he really means is, “I am afraid you no longer love me.”
A wife may say, “All you care about is sex,” when what she really means is, “I am afraid you only notice me when you want something.”
Neither sentence necessarily tells the whole story.
Both may be cries from wounded hearts.
And the tragedy is that two people can spend years defending themselves against accusations when what they actually need is a safe place to tell the truth.
Perhaps the most painful thing about marital distance is not always the absence of touch.
Sometimes it is the absence of tenderness.
The hand that no longer reaches across the table.
The apology that never comes.
The conversation that ends before anything honest is said.
The spouse who feels like a burden.
The spouse who feels invisible.
The marriage that still functions but no longer feels like a friendship.
And this is why Paul's words should never be isolated from the wider teaching of Scripture.
First Corinthians 13 reminds us that love is patient and kind, does not insist on its own way, and does not rejoice in wrongdoing.
Colossians 3:19 tells husbands not to be harsh with their wives.
First Peter 3:7 calls husbands to live with their wives in an understanding way and honor them.
Ephesians 4:32 calls believers to kindness, tenderheartedness, and forgiveness.
These passages do not cancel 1 Corinthians 7.
They help us obey it rightly.
The Bible does not offer a vision of marriage where one spouse's desires automatically outweigh the other's well-being.
It calls married believers to a love shaped by the character of Christ.
And Christ never confused love with selfish domination.
Now imagine a different kind of bedroom conversation.
Not an argument over who is right.
Not a demand disguised as a Bible study.
Not another night of resentment.
Just a husband sitting beside his wife and saying, “I miss us. But I don't want you to feel pressured. I want to understand what has happened between us.”
Imagine a wife looking at her husband and saying, “I know we have grown distant. I have been carrying things I never told you. Can we begin again?”
Imagine two people admitting that their marriage has not been what it should be.
Not pretending.
Not accusing.
Not using God as a weapon.
Just telling the truth.
Perhaps there are tears.
Perhaps the conversation is awkward.
Perhaps the wounds are too deep for one evening to resolve.
Perhaps they need a trusted pastor, a qualified marriage counselor, or a healthcare professional.
And perhaps reconciliation will take far longer than either hoped.
But there is something sacred about choosing truth over performance.
Because healing rarely begins with pretending nothing is wrong.
It often begins when someone finally says, “Something is broken, and we need help.”
And for Christians, that confession points toward the very heart of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity had everything under control.
He came because sin had entered the world and we could not rescue ourselves.
He came for people who had failed.
People who had betrayed trust.
People who carried shame.
People who were weary from trying to appear righteous while hiding their wounds.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
That is grace.
Not permission to continue harming others.
Not a religious covering for unrepentant behavior.
Grace calls us out of darkness.
Grace teaches us to confess.
Grace teaches us to forgive.
Grace teaches us to change.
And the same Jesus who forgives sin also calls sinners to repentance.
Maybe you are reading this as a husband who has been selfish.
Maybe you have been more concerned about what you believe you deserve than whether your wife feels cherished.
You know the verses about marital responsibility, but you have neglected the verses about sacrificial love.
If that is you, do not defend what God is exposing.
Repent.
Ask forgiveness without demanding immediate reassurance.
Learn to listen.
Let your actions demonstrate the change your words promise.
Or perhaps you are a wife who has allowed bitterness to grow into deliberate punishment.
Maybe you stopped communicating honestly and began using distance to express what you were too hurt or angry to say.
If that is your situation, ask God for the courage to address the real wound.
But if you have withdrawn because of fear, pain, trauma, exhaustion, or mistreatment, do not mistake your need for safety and healing for rebellion against God.
Your suffering matters.
Your voice matters.
And seeking help is not a betrayal of your faith.
Maybe you are the spouse who has been rejected for so long that you no longer know how to ask for affection.
You have started wondering whether something is wrong with you.
You look in the mirror and feel less desirable than you once did.
You compare yourself with people you see online.
You question whether your marriage will ever feel warm again.
Please hear this.
Your worth was never established by how often someone desires you.
Your worth is not measured by another person's responsiveness.
You were made in the image of God.
And if you belong to Christ, your deepest identity rests in Him.
A wounded marriage can affect your confidence.
It does not have the authority to define your value.
There is also something important that Paul says later in the chapter.
In 1 Corinthians 7:6, he explains that he is speaking by way of concession, not command.
Interpreters debate the precise scope of that statement, but it is a reminder that this chapter requires careful reading.
Paul is giving pastoral instruction to real believers facing real circumstances.
He is not writing a mechanical formula that removes the need for wisdom, compassion, or discernment.
And when he speaks of marriage in verse 7, he acknowledges that people have different gifts from God.
Paul himself values singleness and celibacy.
He does not teach that marriage is the only faithful Christian life.
Nor does he teach that sexual activity is the measure of spiritual maturity.
That is important because Christians sometimes elevate marriage so highly that unmarried believers are made to feel incomplete.
But Jesus Christ is sufficient for the single believer, the widowed believer, and the married believer alike.
Our ultimate hope is not found in sexual fulfillment.
It is found in Him.
And that truth also protects marriage from becoming an idol.
Your spouse cannot be your savior.
Your spouse cannot heal every wound in your soul.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of expectations that belong to God alone.
A healthy marriage is not two perfect people satisfying every need without difficulty.
It is two imperfect people learning, through God's grace, to love faithfully in the reality of human weakness.
Sometimes that means rebuilding trust.
Sometimes it means pursuing medical treatment.
Sometimes it means confessing sin.
Sometimes it means respecting necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it means learning how to express affection without expecting every embrace to lead to sex.
Sometimes it means praying together after years of spiritual distance.
And sometimes, where there has been serious harm, it means accepting that repentance must be demonstrated through sustained change and that reconciliation cannot be forced.
Not every marriage story ends with the restoration we hoped for.
We should never promise that one prayer, one conversation, or one act of repentance will guarantee a particular outcome.
But we can proclaim something Scripture does promise.
Christ is faithful.
He is near to the brokenhearted, as Psalm 34:18 teaches.
He gives grace to the humble, as James 4:6 reminds us.
And He calls His people to walk in the light rather than hide in darkness.
That is why the Gospel is bigger than a repaired marriage.
It is the good news that sinners can be reconciled to God through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And from that reconciliation flows the possibility of a transformed life.
A life where pride begins to surrender.
Where confession replaces denial.
Where kindness replaces cruelty.
Where patience replaces entitlement.
Where truth replaces secrecy.
Where forgiveness is offered without pretending that wrongdoing never happened.
And where love begins to look less like taking and more like giving.
So why did Paul warn married couples against depriving one another except by mutual agreement?
Because he understood that marriage involves mutual responsibilities.
Because he rejected the idea that one spouse could unilaterally disregard the other while claiming spiritual superiority.
Because he recognized that prolonged abstinence could become a source of temptation in some marriages.
Because marital intimacy, rightly understood, belongs within a covenant of mutual care.
And because Christian marriage must be governed by something greater than individual appetite.
It must be shaped by love.
Not love as a sentimental feeling.
Not love as a bargaining tool.
Not love as an excuse for control.
But love that honors God by seeking the genuine good of another person.
That is the lesson we cannot afford to miss.
The question is not simply, “Am I receiving what I want from my spouse?”
The deeper question is, “Am I loving my spouse in a way that reflects the character of Jesus Christ?”
And that question has the power to expose both selfish demands and selfish neglect.
It can challenge the person who insists.
It can challenge the person who punishes.
It can challenge the person who refuses to listen.
And it can invite two wounded people to seek something better than victory over each other.
Not every marriage will be healed overnight.
Some wounds take years.
Some require professional intervention.
Some situations require distance for protection.
And some consequences remain even after genuine repentance.
But no Christian marriage becomes healthier by using Scripture to justify cruelty.
The Word of God is not a weapon for winning control of your spouse.
It is truth that calls both of you to stand before the Lord.
And perhaps the most important thing you can do after reading this is not to send the article to your spouse with the words, “See? I told you.”
Perhaps it is to sit quietly before God and ask:
“Lord, what are You showing me about my own heart?”
Not your husband's heart.
Not your wife's heart.
Yours.
Because transformation often begins when we stop using the Bible only to examine someone else.
If this article has exposed pride, bitterness, neglect, fear, or spiritual confusion in your life, do not bury that conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to apologize, apologize.
If you need help, seek it.
If you need protection, do not allow religious pressure to keep you in danger.
And if you are exhausted from carrying a marriage wound nobody sees, remember that you are not invisible to God.
I want to ask you something, and I hope you will answer with sincerity.
What do you believe destroys intimacy more deeply in marriage: physical distance, unresolved resentment, or the feeling that your spouse no longer understands you?
There are people reading who may need the same reminder you needed today.
A husband who has confused biblical leadership with control.
A wife who has quietly lost hope.
A couple who have not spoken honestly in years.
A newlywed who needs to learn the difference between covenant intimacy and entitlement before serious wounds develop.
We are building more than a collection of inspirational posts.

We want to cultivate a community where people can encounter the Gospel, examine Scripture carefully, grow in discipleship, and find encouragement to follow Christ faithfully in the ordinary struggles of life.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible to people who may never be able to purchase a Christian book or pay for a discipleship resource.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or encouraged you during a difficult season, I want to invite you to consider something meaningful.

You can prayerfully treat that support as part of your personal Christian generosity and offering, while remembering that the biblical tithe and the responsibilities you have toward your local church deserve thoughtful, faithful consideration.
You can glorify Him through obedience, generosity, service, prayer, sharing the Gospel, and countless acts of love.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
More Scripture reaching more homes.
More believers being equipped to recognize biblical truth.
More people being reminded that their past does not have to be the final word over their future.
More hearts being pointed toward Jesus Christ.
Because the goal has never been to build an audience that simply admires powerful words.
The goal is to point people toward the Savior who changes lives.
The Savior who confronts sin without abandoning the repentant.
The Savior who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The Savior who teaches husbands to love sacrificially, wives and husbands to honor one another, wounded people to seek healing, and every believer to find their deepest hope in Him.
And before you leave, remember this.
Paul's warning in 1 Corinthians 7:5 is not an invitation to demand more from your spouse while giving less of yourself.
It is a call to take your covenant seriously, to recognize your mutual responsibilities, and to refuse the kind of selfishness that turns love into a struggle for power.
Your marriage may have a history you wish you could erase.
Perhaps there have been bitter arguments.
Long seasons of silence.
Broken promises.
Moments of shame.
Mistakes that still hurt when you remember them.
But the Gospel tells us that our greatest hope is not found in pretending the past never happened.
Our hope is in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ, who forgives sinners, transforms hearts, and teaches His people to walk in newness of life.
And even when a particular relationship cannot be restored, His grace remains sufficient for the person who turns to Him.
So do not make 1 Corinthians 7:5 a weapon.
Let it become an invitation to humility.
Let it move you toward honest conversation.
Let it remind you that love is not merely about what you receive, but also about how faithfully you give.
And above all, let it lead you back to Jesus.
Because the deepest tragedy is not always two people sleeping far apart—it is two hearts forgetting how to love while still lying beside each other.
